cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Counting Apples
cards.question: A fruit seller has 4 apples and buys 3 more. How many apples now?
cards.explanation: Adding means putting groups together and counting the total: 4 + 3 = 7.
cards.realWorldExample: Shopkeepers add up items all day — counting stock, billing customers, and restocking shelves.
cards.funFact: The "+" sign was first used in print in 1489!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Shape Detective
cards.question: A slice of pizza (before it's cut round) and a road sign warning of danger both look like which shape?
cards.explanation: A triangle has 3 straight sides and 3 corners.
cards.realWorldExample: Triangles are used in bridges and roofs because their shape makes them very strong and hard to bend.
cards.funFact: The Great Pyramid of Giza is basically 4 giant triangles meeting at a point!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Coin Count
cards.question: You have 10 one-rupee coins. How many groups of 2 can you make?
cards.explanation: Splitting 10 into groups of 2 is an early form of division: 10 ÷ 2 = 5.
cards.realWorldExample: Sharing a packet of biscuits equally among friends uses the exact same idea.
cards.funFact: Division is really just "fast subtraction" done again and again!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Reading Clocks
cards.question: When the short hand points to 3 and the long hand points to 12, what time is it?
cards.explanation: The short hand shows the hour, and the long hand at 12 means "o'clock" — exactly 3:00.
cards.realWorldExample: You use this every day to know when school starts, or when your favourite cartoon comes on!
cards.funFact: Before clocks, people told time using sundials and shadows.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Bigger or Smaller
cards.question: Your pencil is 14 cm long and your eraser is 5 cm long. How much longer is the pencil?
cards.explanation: Comparing lengths uses subtraction: 14 − 5 = 9 cm.
cards.realWorldExample: Tailors subtract measurements like this every time they cut cloth to fit you.
cards.funFact: Ancient Egyptians measured length using their own forearms, called a "cubit"!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Odd One Out
cards.question: You have 7 candies and want to share them equally between 2 friends with none left over. Can you?
choices: No, 7 is an odd number so one will be left over
cards.explanation: Odd numbers like 7 cannot be split into two exactly equal whole groups — one candy will always be left over.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why sharing an odd number of sweets or seats among two people always ends with someone getting one extra or asking to split it.
cards.funFact: Every other counting number is odd or even, alternating forever — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5...!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Who's First?
cards.question: In a race, Meera finishes before Raj, and Raj finishes before Sam. Who finishes in 2nd place?
cards.explanation: Ordering positions (1st, 2nd, 3rd) is called using ordinal numbers — here the order is Meera, then Raj, then Sam.
cards.realWorldExample: Sports podiums, exam rank lists, and even queue positions at a shop all use this exact idea of ordering.
cards.funFact: The Olympics only give medals for 1st, 2nd, and 3rd place — gold, silver, and bronze!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Pizza Fractions
cards.question: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. You eat 3. What fraction is left?
cards.realWorldExample: Recipes use fractions constantly — like needing 3/4 cup of flour for a cake.
cards.funFact: Ancient Egyptians used only "unit fractions" (like 1/2, 1/3) — no other kind!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Shopping Change
cards.question: A notebook costs ₹35. You pay with a ₹50 note. How much change do you get?
cards.explanation: Change = amount paid − price = 50 − 35 = ₹15.
cards.realWorldExample: Cashiers calculate this instantly every time you buy something at a store.
cards.funFact: The rupee symbol ₹ was officially adopted by India only in 2010!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Perimeter Puzzle
cards.question: A rectangular garden is 6 m long and 4 m wide. What fence length is needed to go all around it?
cards.explanation: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width) = 2 × (6 + 4) = 20 m.
cards.realWorldExample: Builders calculate perimeter to know how much fencing or boundary wall material to buy.
cards.funFact: A running track's inner lane is exactly 400 m — precisely measured perimeter!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Average Runs
cards.question: A cricketer scores 20, 30, and 40 runs in 3 matches. What is the average score?
cards.explanation: Average = total ÷ count = (20+30+40) ÷ 3 = 90 ÷ 3 = 30.
cards.realWorldExample: Sports commentators use batting/bowling averages to compare players all the time.
cards.funFact: Cricket's "average" statistic dates back to the 1700s in England!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Map Scale
cards.question: On a map, 1 cm represents 5 km. How many real km does 4 cm on the map represent?
cards.explanation: Multiply the scale: 4 cm × 5 km/cm = 20 km.
cards.realWorldExample: GPS apps and paper maps both rely on scale to show huge distances on a small screen or page.
cards.funFact: The largest accurate scale map ever made was 1:1 — an actual size map of England (impossible to unfold)!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Reading a Rainfall Chart
cards.question: A bar graph shows rainfall of 20mm, 45mm, and 15mm over three days. Which day had the most rain?
cards.explanation: On a bar graph, the tallest bar represents the largest value — here Day 2's 45mm bar is the tallest.
cards.realWorldExample: Weather reports, news channels, and school science projects all use bar graphs exactly like this to show data at a glance.
cards.funFact: The bar graph was invented by William Playfair in 1786 — he also invented the pie chart!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Packing Pencils
cards.question: A box holds 12 pencils. How many pencils are in 6 boxes?
cards.explanation: Multiplication is repeated addition: 12 pencils × 6 boxes = 72 pencils.
cards.realWorldExample: Shopkeepers use multiplication like this to quickly count stock arriving in sealed cartons.
cards.funFact: The multiplication symbol "×" was first used in a math book printed in 1631!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Discount Day
cards.question: A shirt costs ₹800 and has a 25% discount. What is the sale price?
cards.realWorldExample: Every "SALE 25% OFF" sign you see in a mall uses this exact calculation.
cards.funFact: The word "percent" comes from Latin "per centum" meaning "by the hundred".

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Balancing Equations
cards.question: Solve for x: 3x + 5 = 20
cards.explanation: Subtract 5 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.
cards.realWorldExample: Engineers solve equations like this to find unknown quantities — like how much material or budget is needed.
cards.funFact: The "=" sign was invented in 1557 because the inventor was tired of writing "is equal to"!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Speed & Ratio
cards.question: A car travels 180 km in 3 hours. What is its speed?
cards.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time = 180 ÷ 3 = 60 km/h.
cards.realWorldExample: Your car's speedometer, flight durations, and delivery time estimates all use this ratio.
cards.funFact: Light travels at about 300,000 km per SECOND — a billion times faster than a car!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Probability Roll
cards.question: What is the probability of rolling a 4 on a standard 6-sided die?
cards.explanation: There is 1 favourable outcome (rolling a 4) out of 6 possible outcomes: 1/6.
cards.realWorldExample: Weather forecasts ("70% chance of rain") and insurance companies both rely on probability.
cards.funFact: Casinos and lotteries are entirely built on the mathematics of probability!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Volume of a Box
cards.question: A box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide, and 5 cm tall. What is its volume?
cards.explanation: Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height = 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 cm³.
cards.realWorldExample: Packaging companies compute volume to fit the most boxes into a delivery truck.
cards.funFact: A standard shipping container holds about 33 cubic metres — that's 33 million cm³!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Scaling a Recipe
cards.question: A cake recipe for 4 people needs 200g of flour. How much flour is needed for 10 people?
cards.explanation: This uses ratio/proportion: 200g ÷ 4 people = 50g per person, so 10 people need 50 × 10 = 500g.
cards.realWorldExample: Bakers and chefs scale recipes up or down this exact way when cooking for more or fewer guests.
cards.funFact: Professional kitchens use ratio recipes (like "1 part sugar to 2 parts flour") so a dish scales perfectly to any size!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Below Zero
cards.question: The temperature is -3°C at night and rises by 8°C by noon. What is the noon temperature?
cards.explanation: Adding a positive number to a negative one: -3 + 8 = 5°C.
cards.realWorldExample: Weather reports in cold countries use negative numbers constantly, and pilots calculate temperature changes at altitude the same way.
cards.funFact: The coldest temperature ever recorded on Earth was -89.2°C, in Antarctica!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Signal Height
cards.question: A mobile tower casts a shadow of 30 m when the sun's angle gives a shadow-to-height ratio of 1:2. How tall is the tower?
cards.explanation: If shadow : height = 1 : 2, then height = 2 × shadow = 2 × 30 = 60 m.
cards.realWorldExample: Surveyors use similar-triangle ratios (trigonometry) to measure towers and mountains without climbing them.
cards.funFact: The ancient Greek Thales measured the Great Pyramid's height this exact way, using shadows!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Quadratic Launch
cards.question: A ball's height follows h = -x² + 4x. At what value of x does it hit the ground again (h=0, x≠0)?
cards.explanation: Set -x² + 4x = 0 → x(4 - x) = 0 → x = 0 or x = 4. The ball lands at x = 4.
cards.realWorldExample: Rocket and projectile engineers use quadratic equations to predict landing points.
cards.funFact: NASA still uses parabolic (quadratic) paths to plan how spacecraft re-enter the atmosphere!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Compound Interest
cards.question: ₹1000 is invested at 10% compound interest per year. What is it worth after 2 years?
cards.realWorldExample: Bank savings accounts, loans, and even population growth models use compound interest formulas.
cards.funFact: Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest "the eighth wonder of the world"!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Data Spread
cards.question: Which measure tells you how "spread out" a set of exam scores is?
cards.explanation: Standard deviation measures how far data points typically are from the average.
cards.realWorldExample: Quality control in factories uses standard deviation to check if products are consistently sized.
cards.funFact: Standard deviation is why exam results are often shown as a "bell curve"!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Prime Power
cards.question: Which of these numbers is prime (only divisible by 1 and itself)?
cards.explanation: 29 cannot be divided evenly by any number except 1 and 29 — it is prime.
cards.realWorldExample: Huge prime numbers secretly protect your online banking and messages through encryption.
cards.funFact: The largest known prime number has over 41 million digits!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Pythagoras's Ladder
cards.question: A 5m ladder leans against a wall with its base 3m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
cards.explanation: By the Pythagorean theorem, height² + 3² = 5², so height² = 25 − 9 = 16, giving height = 4m.
cards.realWorldExample: Builders and electricians use exactly this calculation to check a ladder is placed at a safe, stable angle.
cards.funFact: The 3-4-5 triangle is so useful that ancient Egyptian builders used a knotted rope with those exact spacings to make perfect right angles!

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Exponential Spread
cards.question: If a rumour is told to 2 new people every hour, and each of those tells 2 more the next hour, what kind of growth is this?
cards.explanation: Exponential growth means the quantity multiplies by a fixed factor each step, growing extremely fast — very different from adding a fixed amount each time (linear growth).
cards.realWorldExample: This is exactly how viral social media posts, chain messages, and disease outbreaks can spread shockingly fast from a small start.
cards.funFact: Starting from just 1 person and doubling every day, you would pass 1 million people in only 20 days!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Push and Pull
cards.question: To open a door, do you usually push it or pull it?
choices: Push or pull depending on the door
cards.explanation: A push and a pull are both forces — they make things move, stop, or change direction.
cards.realWorldExample: Swings, doors, and shopping trolleys all move because of pushes and pulls.
cards.funFact: Even a magnet pulling a paperclip is an invisible force at work!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Shadow Play
cards.question: What do you need to make a shadow?
cards.explanation: A shadow forms when an object blocks light from reaching a surface.
cards.realWorldExample: Sundials, shadow puppet shows, and even your own shadow at the park use this idea.
cards.funFact: Your shadow is shortest at noon when the sun is directly overhead!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Magnet Magic
cards.question: Which of these objects would a magnet attract?
cards.explanation: Magnets attract certain metals like iron and steel — a paper clip is usually made of steel.
cards.realWorldExample: Fridge magnets, compasses, and recycling machines that sort metal all use magnetism.
cards.funFact: The Earth itself is a giant magnet — that's why compasses always point north!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Melting Ice
cards.question: What happens to an ice cube left out on a warm table?
cards.explanation: Heat from the warm air makes the solid ice change into liquid water — this is called melting.
cards.realWorldExample: This is exactly why ice cream melts fast on a hot day if you don't eat it quickly!
cards.funFact: Water is one of the few substances where its solid form (ice) floats on its liquid form!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Sound Travels
cards.question: How does sound reach your ears when someone claps?
cards.explanation: A clap makes the air vibrate, and those vibrations travel to your ear as sound.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why you can hear a friend talking across the room, and why drums make a "boom".
cards.funFact: Sound cannot travel in space because there is no air to vibrate!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Stretchy Things
cards.question: What happens to a rubber band when you stop stretching it?
choices: It springs back to its original shape
cards.explanation: An elastic material like rubber stretches under force but springs back to its original shape once you let go.
cards.realWorldExample: Rubber bands, elastic waistbands, and trampolines all rely on this springing-back property.
cards.funFact: A trampoline's bounce comes from its springs and fabric stretching and snapping back super fast!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Hot Spoon
cards.question: Why does a metal spoon left in hot soup become warm all the way up its handle?
choices: The spoon makes its own heat
The soup jumps onto the handle
It only feels warm, but is not
cards.explanation: Metal is a good conductor of heat — heat energy travels through it from the hot part to the cooler part.
cards.realWorldExample: This is exactly why cooking pots have wooden or plastic handles — those materials conduct heat poorly, so they stay cool to hold.
cards.funFact: Metal feels colder than wood at the same room temperature simply because it conducts heat away from your hand faster!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Simple Machines
cards.question: A seesaw at the park is an example of which simple machine?
cards.explanation: A lever pivots around a fixed point (fulcrum) to lift a load — exactly like a seesaw.
cards.realWorldExample: Scissors, bottle openers, and crowbars are all levers used in everyday life.
cards.funFact: Archimedes said, "Give me a lever long enough and I can move the Earth!"

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Rainbow Science
cards.question: A rainbow appears when sunlight passes through what?
cards.explanation: Raindrops split (refract) white sunlight into its rainbow of colours.
cards.realWorldExample: You can make a mini rainbow at home using a garden hose spray on a sunny day.
cards.funFact: A rainbow is actually a full circle — from the ground we only see the top arc!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Floating and Sinking
cards.question: Why does a helium balloon float up in the air?
choices: It is pushed by wind only
cards.explanation: Helium gas is less dense than the surrounding air, so the balloon rises.
cards.realWorldExample: Weather balloons and blimps use lighter-than-air gases to float high in the sky.
cards.funFact: A regular party balloon filled with your breath sinks — because your breath is mostly heavier gases!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Friction Force
cards.question: Why do bicycle brakes make the wheel stop?
choices: Friction between brake pad and wheel
cards.explanation: The brake pad rubs against the wheel, and friction converts motion into heat, slowing it down.
cards.realWorldExample: Car brakes, shoe soles gripping the floor, and even matchsticks lighting all use friction.
cards.funFact: Without friction, you wouldn't even be able to walk — your feet would just slide!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: States of Matter
cards.question: When water boils and turns to steam, which state change is happening?
cards.explanation: Boiling adds enough heat energy for liquid water molecules to escape as gas (steam).
cards.realWorldExample: A kettle whistling, or fog rising off a hot cup of tea, both show liquid turning to gas.
cards.funFact: On top of Mount Everest, water boils at a much lower temperature because air pressure is lower!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Sharp vs Blunt
cards.question: Why does a sharp knife cut through food much more easily than a blunt one, using the same push?
choices: A sharp edge focuses force onto a tiny area, increasing pressure
Blunt knives are made of weaker metal
cards.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area. A sharp edge has a very small area, so the same force creates much higher pressure, cutting more easily.
cards.realWorldExample: This is also why drawing pins and needles have sharp points — to concentrate force into a tiny area to pierce through material.
cards.funFact: Snowshoes work on the opposite idea — spreading your weight over a large area to lower pressure, so you don't sink into snow!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Oil on Water
cards.question: Why does cooking oil float on top of water instead of mixing in?
choices: Oil is less dense than water
cards.explanation: Oil has a lower density than water, meaning it weighs less for the same volume, so it floats on top instead of sinking or mixing.
cards.realWorldExample: This is exactly why oil spills in the ocean spread out as a floating layer on the sea surface instead of sinking.
cards.funFact: Density is also why a can of regular soda sinks in water, but a can of diet soda (with less sugar) often floats!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Newton's First Law
cards.question: A ball rolling on a frictionless floor would keep moving forever unless...
cards.explanation: Newton's First Law: an object stays at rest or in motion unless acted on by an external force.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why you jerk forward in a car that suddenly brakes — your body wants to keep moving.
cards.funFact: Seatbelts exist specifically to provide the force that stops your body from this exact effect!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Energy Conversion
cards.question: A solar panel converts sunlight into which form of energy?
cards.explanation: Solar panels use the photovoltaic effect to convert light energy directly into electrical energy.
cards.realWorldExample: Solar-powered calculators, streetlights, and rooftop panels all rely on this conversion.
cards.funFact: The International Space Station is powered almost entirely by giant solar panel wings!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Force = Mass × Acceleration
cards.question: If you push a shopping cart with the same force, which is easier to speed up — an empty cart or a full one?
cards.explanation: Newton's Second Law: F = ma. With less mass, the same force produces greater acceleration.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why an empty truck accelerates faster than a fully loaded one with the same engine power.
cards.funFact: Formula 1 cars are built ultra-light for exactly this reason — less mass, faster acceleration!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Newton's Third Law
cards.question: A rocket launches upward by pushing gas downward. This is an example of...
choices: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
cards.explanation: Newton's Third Law: the rocket pushes gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up with equal force.
cards.realWorldExample: Swimming works the same way — you push water backward, and it pushes you forward.
cards.funFact: A squid actually "jets" through water using this same action-reaction principle!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Reflection and Lenses
cards.question: What type of lens is used in a magnifying glass to make things look bigger?
cards.explanation: A convex lens bends light rays inward, magnifying the image of an object.
cards.realWorldExample: Magnifying glasses, camera lenses, and eyeglasses for far-sightedness all use convex lenses.
cards.funFact: Galileo used convex and concave lenses together to build one of the first telescopes!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Pressure Underwater
cards.question: Why are dams built much thicker at the bottom than at the top?
choices: Water pressure increases with depth, so the base must withstand much greater force
cards.explanation: Water pressure increases the deeper you go, so the bottom of a dam must be far stronger to hold back that much greater force.
cards.realWorldExample: Deep-sea submarines are built with extremely thick, rounded hulls for the same reason — to survive crushing pressure at depth.
cards.funFact: At the deepest point of the ocean (about 11 km down), pressure is over 1,000 times what you feel at the surface!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Swinging Pendulum
cards.question: What mainly determines how long it takes a simple pendulum to swing back and forth once?
cards.explanation: A pendulum's swing time depends mainly on its length (longer swings take longer), not on the weight of the bob.
cards.realWorldExample: Old grandfather clocks use a pendulum of a precisely set length to tick at a steady, reliable rate.
cards.funFact: Galileo reportedly discovered this timing property by watching a swinging chandelier in a cathedral, using his own pulse to time it!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Work and Power
cards.question: Two people lift identical boxes to the same height, but one does it faster. Who has more power?
cards.explanation: Power = Work ÷ Time. Doing the same work in less time means greater power.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why a sports car engine (high power) can accelerate faster than a truck engine doing the same work.
cards.funFact: The unit "horsepower" was coined by James Watt to compare steam engines to actual horses!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Wave Frequency
cards.question: A siren sounds higher pitched as an ambulance approaches you and lower as it drives away. What is this called?
cards.explanation: The Doppler effect happens because sound waves compress as the source approaches and stretch as it moves away.
cards.realWorldExample: Police radar guns and weather radar (for storms) both use the Doppler effect to measure speed.
cards.funFact: The Doppler effect also happens with light — it helps astronomers tell if stars are moving toward or away from us!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Laws of Thermodynamics
cards.question: Why does a hot cup of tea eventually cool down to room temperature, but a cold glass of water never spontaneously boils itself?
choices: Heat naturally flows from hot to cold
cards.explanation: The Second Law of Thermodynamics states heat flows naturally from a hotter object to a colder one, not the reverse.
cards.realWorldExample: This is exactly why refrigerators need to do extra work (using electricity) to pump heat out against this natural flow.
cards.funFact: This law is also why perpetual motion machines are physically impossible!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Electromagnetic Spectrum
cards.question: Which of these is NOT part of the electromagnetic spectrum?
cards.explanation: Sound waves are mechanical vibrations needing a medium; electromagnetic waves (light, X-rays, radio) can travel through vacuum.
cards.realWorldExample: Wi-Fi, microwaves for cooking, and hospital X-ray machines all use different parts of this same spectrum.
cards.funFact: Visible light — everything you can see — is less than 1% of the entire electromagnetic spectrum!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Gravitational Pull
cards.question: Why do astronauts float inside the International Space Station even though Earth's gravity still acts on them there?
choices: There is no gravity in space
They are in constant free-fall around Earth
cards.explanation: The ISS and astronauts are continuously falling toward Earth but moving forward fast enough to keep missing it — orbiting.
cards.realWorldExample: This is the same idea as throwing a ball so fast it never comes back down — just applied to a space station!
cards.funFact: The ISS travels at about 28,000 km/h — fast enough to orbit Earth every 90 minutes!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Nuclear Fission
cards.question: How do nuclear power plants generate electricity?
choices: By splitting atomic nuclei to release heat, which boils water into steam to spin turbines
cards.explanation: Nuclear fission splits heavy atoms (like uranium), releasing huge amounts of heat that boils water into steam, which spins turbines connected to generators.
cards.realWorldExample: Countries like France generate most of their electricity this way, producing large amounts of power without burning fossil fuels.
cards.funFact: Splitting just 1 kg of uranium releases roughly as much energy as burning about 2,700 tonnes of coal!

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Crumple Zones
cards.question: Why are modern car fronts designed to crumple and collapse during a crash, instead of staying perfectly rigid?
choices: To make cars cheaper to build
To extend the collision time, reducing the force experienced by passengers
Crumpling is just an accident of design, not intentional
cards.explanation: By Newton's laws, spreading a crash's force over more time (as the front crumples) reduces the peak force passengers feel, thanks to the impulse-momentum relationship.
cards.realWorldExample: This crumple-zone design, combined with seatbelts and airbags, is a major reason car crash survival rates have improved dramatically since the 1960s.
cards.funFact: Formula 1 cars use the same idea — their nose cones are designed to shatter apart on impact, absorbing crash energy away from the driver!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Torch Power
cards.question: What makes a torch light up when you press its switch?
choices: A battery sending electricity to the bulb
cards.explanation: The battery stores energy and pushes electricity through the switch to light the bulb.
cards.realWorldExample: Every torch, remote control, and toy car uses a battery this same way.
cards.funFact: The first battery was invented in 1800 by Alessandro Volta — that's why we call the unit "volt"!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Switch It On
cards.question: What does a switch do in an electric circuit?
choices: Opens or closes the path for electricity
cards.explanation: A switch either connects (closes) or breaks (opens) the circuit, turning the device on or off.
cards.realWorldExample: Every light switch on your wall works exactly this way.
cards.funFact: The first practical light switch was patented in 1884!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Conductors vs Insulators
cards.question: Which material would you NOT want touching a live electric wire?
cards.explanation: Your body (with moisture and salts) conducts electricity well, so bare hands are dangerous near live wires.
cards.realWorldExample: Electricians wear rubber gloves and use plastic-handled tools because rubber and plastic are insulators.
cards.funFact: Birds can safely sit on a single power line because electricity always looks for the easiest path — through both feet, not through the bird's body!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Battery Basics
cards.question: What happens to a torch when its battery runs out?
cards.explanation: A battery stores a limited amount of energy — once used up, it can no longer push electricity through the circuit.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why your TV remote stops working until you replace its batteries.
cards.funFact: Rechargeable batteries can be "refilled" with energy hundreds of times!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Complete the Circuit
cards.question: For a bulb to light up, the wires must form what kind of path?
cards.explanation: Electricity needs a complete, closed loop (circuit) from the battery, through the bulb, and back.
cards.realWorldExample: If a single wire in your string of fairy lights breaks, sometimes the whole string goes dark!
cards.funFact: The word "circuit" comes from a Latin word meaning "to go around"!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Reusable Power
cards.question: What is special about a rechargeable battery compared to a normal one-time-use battery?
choices: It can be refilled with energy and used again many times
It never runs out at all
cards.explanation: A rechargeable battery can be plugged into a charger to refill its stored energy, so it can be used hundreds of times instead of being thrown away.
cards.realWorldExample: Phones, laptops, and electric cars all use rechargeable batteries so you don't need to buy new ones constantly.
cards.funFact: Using rechargeable batteries instead of disposable ones helps reduce a huge amount of battery waste every year!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Invisible Remote Signal
cards.question: How does a TV remote control tell the TV to change channels without any wires?
choices: It sends an invisible infrared light signal
It pushes air toward the TV
cards.explanation: A TV remote sends a pattern of invisible infrared light pulses that a sensor on the TV detects and understands as a command.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why a remote must usually point roughly at the TV to work — infrared light travels in a fairly straight line.
cards.funFact: You can often see a remote's infrared light flashing if you look at its bulb through a phone camera — infrared is invisible to human eyes but not to most camera sensors!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Series Circuits
cards.question: In a series circuit with two bulbs, what happens if one bulb burns out?
cards.explanation: In a series circuit, there is only one path — if it breaks anywhere, current stops flowing everywhere.
cards.realWorldExample: Old-style Christmas lights were wired in series — one bulb dies and the whole string goes out!
cards.funFact: Modern fairy lights use parallel wiring specifically to avoid this problem.

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Parallel Circuits
cards.question: Why are the lights in your house wired in parallel, not series?
choices: So one broken light doesn't turn off all the others
It is required by law only
cards.explanation: In a parallel circuit, each device has its own path, so one failing doesn't affect the others.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why turning off your bedroom light doesn't switch off the kitchen light too.
cards.funFact: Your home's entire electrical wiring is one giant parallel circuit!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Electromagnets
cards.question: What can turn a plain iron nail into a temporary magnet?
choices: Wrapping it with coiled wire carrying electric current
cards.explanation: Coiling a current-carrying wire around iron creates a magnetic field — an electromagnet.
cards.realWorldExample: Junkyard cranes use giant electromagnets to lift and drop scrap cars and metal.
cards.funFact: You can switch an electromagnet off just by cutting the electricity — unlike a regular magnet!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Sensors All Around
cards.question: A streetlight that turns on automatically at dusk is using what kind of sensor?
cards.explanation: A Light Dependent Resistor (LDR) senses darkness and completes the circuit to switch the light on.
cards.realWorldExample: Automatic streetlights, some garden lamps, and even your phone's auto-brightness use light sensors.
cards.funFact: LDRs are made from a material called cadmium sulfide that reacts to light!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Fuses and Safety
cards.question: What is the job of a fuse in an electrical circuit?
choices: Break the circuit if too much current flows, preventing fire
cards.explanation: A fuse contains a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if current gets dangerously high, protecting devices and homes.
cards.realWorldExample: Your home's fuse box (or circuit breaker) protects all your appliances from electrical surges.
cards.funFact: Modern homes mostly use circuit breakers instead of fuses because they can be reset instead of replaced!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Spinning Fans
cards.question: What makes an electric fan's blades spin when you switch it on?
choices: A tiny electric motor converts electrical energy into spinning motion
The battery pushes the blades directly
It uses magnets to freeze the air
cards.explanation: An electric motor uses electricity and magnetism together to create spinning (rotational) motion, turning the fan's blades.
cards.realWorldExample: Fans, washing machines, and electric toothbrushes all contain small motors doing this same job.
cards.funFact: A single large wind turbine works like a giant fan in reverse — wind spins the blades to generate electricity instead of the other way around!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Static Cling
cards.question: Why does a balloon rubbed on your hair stick to a wall afterward?
choices: Rubbing builds up static electric charge that attracts the wall
cards.explanation: Rubbing the balloon transfers electric charge onto its surface, and this static charge attracts it to the neutral wall.
cards.realWorldExample: This same static buildup is why your hair sometimes stands up after pulling off a wool sweater.
cards.funFact: Lightning is actually a giant, dramatic version of the same static electricity effect, built up inside storm clouds!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Ohm's Law
cards.question: Using Ohm's Law (V = IR), if voltage is 12V and resistance is 4Ω, what is the current?
cards.explanation: Rearranging V = IR gives I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A.
cards.realWorldExample: Electricians use Ohm's Law to safely calculate wiring and appliance ratings.
cards.funFact: Georg Ohm was so criticized for his theory in 1827 that he initially resigned from his teaching job!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Resistors and Color Codes
cards.question: Why do circuits use resistors?
choices: To control/limit the flow of current
cards.explanation: Resistors limit current flow to protect components like LEDs from burning out.
cards.realWorldExample: Every LED circuit — from toy lights to TV remotes — includes a resistor to prevent the LED from getting too much current.
cards.funFact: Resistors use colored bands as a code so you can read their value without any equipment!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: LED Efficiency
cards.question: Why have LED bulbs largely replaced old incandescent bulbs in homes?
choices: LEDs use much less energy for the same brightness
cards.explanation: LEDs convert most electrical energy into light rather than wasted heat, making them far more efficient.
cards.realWorldExample: Switching your home to LED bulbs can cut lighting electricity costs by up to 80%.
cards.funFact: A modern LED bulb can last over 25,000 hours — nearly 3 years of continuous use!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: AC vs DC
cards.question: What type of current comes out of a standard household wall socket?
cards.explanation: Household power is Alternating Current (AC), which reverses direction many times per second, unlike a battery's steady DC.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why phone chargers contain an adapter — to convert wall AC power into the DC power your phone battery needs.
cards.funFact: The "War of Currents" in the 1880s between Edison (DC) and Tesla (AC) decided how we power our homes today — AC won!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Transistors
cards.question: What is the main job of a transistor in electronic devices?
choices: To act as a tiny switch or amplifier
cards.explanation: Transistors switch or amplify electronic signals, forming the building blocks of all modern digital devices.
cards.realWorldExample: Your smartphone contains billions of transistors packed onto a single chip smaller than a fingernail.
cards.funFact: The first transistor, built in 1947, was about the size of a hand — now billions fit on one chip!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Solar Power Banks
cards.question: A portable power bank with a solar panel charges your phone even without a wall socket. How?
choices: It stores wind instead of electricity
The panel converts sunlight into electricity, which charges the power bank's internal battery
It uses the Sun's heat as fuel directly
cards.explanation: A solar panel converts light energy into electrical energy, which charges the power bank's battery for later use, even away from mains power.
cards.realWorldExample: Hikers and campers use solar power banks and solar chargers to keep devices running far from any electrical outlet.
cards.funFact: Some solar-powered road signs and calculators have run for years without ever needing a replacement battery!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Capacitors and Camera Flash
cards.question: Why can an old camera's flash light up so brightly and instantly, even though its battery is small?
choices: The battery is secretly very powerful
A capacitor slowly stores charge, then releases it all at once in a sudden burst
The flash bulb makes its own electricity
It uses static electricity from the air
cards.explanation: A capacitor stores electrical charge over a short time and then discharges it almost instantly, delivering a burst of power much greater than the battery could give alone.
cards.realWorldExample: Defibrillators (used to restart a heart in emergencies) work the same way — slowly charging a capacitor, then releasing a powerful, controlled shock.
cards.funFact: Unlike batteries, capacitors can charge and discharge extremely quickly, which is why camera flashes recharge again within seconds!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Semiconductors
cards.question: Why is silicon so important in modern electronics?
choices: It is a semiconductor whose conductivity can be precisely controlled
cards.explanation: Silicon's conductivity can be finely tuned by adding impurities (doping), making it ideal for chips.
cards.realWorldExample: Every computer chip, smartphone processor, and solar panel relies on engineered silicon semiconductors.
cards.funFact: Silicon Valley in California is literally named after this element because of the chip industry based there!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Logic Gates
cards.question: An AND logic gate outputs "1" (true) only when...
cards.explanation: An AND gate requires every input to be true (1) for the output to be true.
cards.realWorldExample: A car might only start (output) if both "key turned" AND "seatbelt on" are true — a real AND gate application.
cards.funFact: All computer processors are built from millions to billions of these simple logic gates combined!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Analog vs Digital Signals
cards.question: What is the key difference between analog and digital signals?
choices: Analog is silent, digital is loud
Analog varies continuously, digital uses discrete steps (0s and 1s)
cards.explanation: Analog signals vary smoothly like a dimmer switch, while digital signals use distinct on/off (binary) values.
cards.realWorldExample: Old vinyl records store analog sound waves directly, while streaming music is digital data (0s and 1s).
cards.funFact: Converting analog sound to digital thousands of times per second is called "sampling" — that's how MP3s are made!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Diodes and Rectifiers
cards.question: What does a diode do in a circuit?
choices: Allows current to flow in only one direction
cards.explanation: A diode is a one-way valve for electric current, essential for converting AC to DC (rectification).
cards.realWorldExample: Every phone charger uses diodes to convert AC wall power into the DC power your phone needs.
cards.funFact: An LED (Light Emitting Diode) is a special diode that gives off light when current flows through it!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Kirchhoff's Laws
cards.question: Kirchhoff's Current Law states that at any junction in a circuit...
choices: Total current entering equals total current leaving
cards.explanation: Kirchhoff's Current Law is based on conservation of charge — current can't be created or destroyed at a junction.
cards.realWorldExample: Engineers use this law to design complex circuit boards like the ones inside your laptop or gaming console.
cards.funFact: Gustav Kirchhoff formulated these laws in 1845 while still a student, at just 21 years old!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Inside a Microchip
cards.question: A modern smartphone processor packs billions of transistors onto a chip smaller than a fingernail. What does this enable?
choices: Nothing extra, it just looks impressive
Extremely fast, complex calculations in a tiny, low-power package
It mainly makes the phone heavier
cards.explanation: Packing billions of tiny transistors together lets a chip perform enormous numbers of calculations per second while staying small and energy-efficient.
cards.realWorldExample: This miniaturization is exactly why a phone in your pocket today is far more powerful than room-sized computers from the 1970s.
cards.funFact: The number of transistors on chips has roughly doubled every two years for decades — a trend called "Moore's Law"!

cards.subject: electronics
cards.title: Wireless Charging
cards.question: How does a wireless charging pad transfer power into a phone without any charging cable plugged in?
choices: It uses Wi-Fi signals to send power
It creates a changing magnetic field that induces current in a coil inside the phone
It heats the phone to charge it
It uses sound waves to transfer energy
cards.explanation: The pad generates a changing magnetic field, which induces an electric current in a matching coil inside the phone — a principle called electromagnetic induction.
cards.realWorldExample: Electric toothbrushes and some electric cars use this same wireless, contact-free charging principle.
cards.funFact: This same induction principle was discovered by Michael Faraday nearly 200 years ago, in 1831!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Day and Night
cards.question: Why do we have day and night?
choices: The Earth spins (rotates) on its axis
The sun turns off at night
cards.explanation: Earth spins once every 24 hours — the side facing the sun has day, the other side has night.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why the sun seems to "rise" in the east and "set" in the west every single day.
cards.funFact: Earth spins at about 1,670 km/h at the equator — faster than a jet plane!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Moon Watching
cards.question: What is the Moon?
choices: Earth's natural satellite that orbits it
cards.explanation: The Moon is a rocky body that orbits Earth, held by gravity, and reflects sunlight.
cards.realWorldExample: You can watch the Moon change shape (phases) throughout the month just by looking up at night.
cards.funFact: The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth — about 3.8 cm every year!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Twinkling Stars
cards.question: What are stars made of?
cards.explanation: Stars are giant balls of extremely hot gas (mostly hydrogen and helium) that glow brightly.
cards.realWorldExample: Our own Sun is a star — just much closer to us than any other star in the sky!
cards.funFact: Stars only appear to "twinkle" because Earth's moving atmosphere bends their light slightly!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Our Home Planet
cards.question: What is special about Earth compared to other planets we know of?
choices: It has liquid water and supports life
It is closest to the Sun
cards.explanation: Earth is the only known planet with liquid water on its surface and living things.
cards.realWorldExample: Astronauts on the Space Station describe Earth as a beautiful "blue marble" surrounded by dark space.
cards.funFact: Earth is the only planet in our solar system not named after a Greek or Roman god!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Sky Watchers
cards.question: What tool do astronomers use to see faraway stars and planets more clearly?
cards.explanation: A telescope collects more light than our eyes can, letting us see distant, faint objects in space.
cards.realWorldExample: The famous Hubble Space Telescope has taken incredible photos of galaxies billions of light-years away.
cards.funFact: Galileo was one of the first people to use a telescope to study the night sky, in 1609!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: The Sun is a Star
cards.question: What does the Sun do for all the planets in our solar system, including Earth?
choices: Its gravity holds the planets in orbit and gives them light and warmth
It is just a big rock
cards.explanation: The Sun sits at the center of our solar system — its gravity keeps every planet in orbit, and its light and heat make life on Earth possible.
cards.realWorldExample: Plants use sunlight to grow through photosynthesis, which is the base of almost every food chain on Earth.
cards.funFact: The Sun is so big that over 1.3 million Earths could fit inside it!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Why Astronauts Wear Suits
cards.question: Why do astronauts need to wear a special space suit outside their spacecraft?
choices: There is no air to breathe and no protection from extreme temperatures in space
cards.explanation: Space has no air to breathe and swings between extreme heat and cold, so a space suit supplies oxygen and protects astronauts from these dangers.
cards.realWorldExample: Space suits also protect astronauts from tiny fast-moving space debris that could otherwise be dangerous.
cards.funFact: A NASA space suit is actually a mini spacecraft by itself, complete with its own oxygen, water, and temperature control!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Moon Phases
cards.question: Why does the Moon appear to change shape throughout the month?
choices: We see different portions of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth
cards.explanation: As the Moon orbits Earth, we see varying amounts of its sunlit side, creating phases from new moon to full moon.
cards.realWorldExample: Many calendars, including Islamic and Chinese calendars, are based on tracking these moon phases.
cards.funFact: A full moon-to-full moon cycle takes about 29.5 days — almost exactly one month!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Why Seasons Change
cards.question: What causes Earth to have seasons like summer and winter?
choices: Earth moving closer and farther from the sun
Earth's tilted axis as it orbits the sun
cards.explanation: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so different parts of Earth get more direct sunlight at different times of year.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why Australia has summer in December while India and the US have winter at the same time!
cards.funFact: Earth is actually slightly CLOSER to the sun during Northern Hemisphere winter — the tilt matters more than distance!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: The Solar System
cards.question: Which planet is known for its spectacular rings?
cards.explanation: Saturn's rings are made of countless chunks of ice and rock orbiting the planet.
cards.realWorldExample: You can actually see Saturn's rings yourself through a basic backyard telescope!
cards.funFact: Saturn is so light for its size that it would actually float in water — if you had a bathtub big enough!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Eclipses Explained
cards.question: What happens during a solar eclipse?
choices: Earth passes between the Sun and Moon
The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, blocking sunlight
cards.explanation: During a solar eclipse, the Moon moves directly between the Sun and Earth, casting a shadow on Earth.
cards.realWorldExample: People travel across the globe just to witness a total solar eclipse where day briefly turns to night!
cards.funFact: A total solar eclipse is possible because the Sun is 400 times bigger than the Moon but also 400 times farther away!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Comets and Asteroids
cards.question: What causes a comet's glowing tail as it nears the Sun?
choices: The Sun's heat vaporizing ice, creating a glowing gas trail
cards.explanation: As a comet approaches the Sun, its icy surface vaporizes, releasing gas and dust that form a glowing tail pushed by solar wind.
cards.realWorldExample: Halley's Comet is famous for returning to be visible from Earth roughly every 76 years.
cards.funFact: A comet's tail always points away from the Sun — not behind the comet's direction of travel!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Shooting Stars
cards.question: What is actually happening when you see a "shooting star" streak across the night sky?
choices: A star is falling out of the sky
A tiny piece of space rock burns up as it enters Earth's atmosphere
A plane is flying with its lights on
cards.explanation: A "shooting star" is actually a small meteoroid burning up from friction as it speeds into Earth's atmosphere, creating a bright streak of light.
cards.realWorldExample: Meteor showers, like the Perseids in August, happen when Earth passes through a trail of dust left behind by a comet.
cards.funFact: Most shooting stars are caused by objects no bigger than a grain of sand or a small pebble!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Floating in Space
cards.question: Why do astronauts float around inside the International Space Station instead of walking normally?
choices: There is no gravity anywhere near Earth
The station and everyone in it are continuously falling around Earth together, feeling weightless
cards.explanation: The station and astronauts are all falling toward Earth at the same rate while moving forward fast enough to keep circling it, which feels like weightlessness.
cards.realWorldExample: This is the same feeling you get for a split second at the top of a rollercoaster drop — just continuous, because the station never actually lands.
cards.funFact: Astronauts can lose bone and muscle strength in long-duration weightlessness, so they must exercise for about 2 hours every single day!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Gravity Holds It Together
cards.question: What force keeps planets orbiting the Sun instead of flying off into space?
cards.explanation: The Sun's immense gravity continuously pulls planets toward it, balancing their forward motion into a stable orbit.
cards.realWorldExample: Satellites orbiting Earth (like GPS satellites) stay up using this exact same gravity-and-motion balance.
cards.funFact: If the Sun's gravity suddenly vanished, Earth would fly off in a straight line at about 107,000 km/h!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Measuring Cosmic Distance
cards.question: What is a "light-year" a measurement of?
choices: The distance light travels in one year
cards.explanation: A light-year measures distance — how far light travels in one year (about 9.46 trillion km).
cards.realWorldExample: When astronomers say a star is "4 light-years away," they mean its light took 4 years to reach us.
cards.funFact: Because light takes time to travel, when you look at distant stars, you're literally looking into the past!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Artificial Satellites
cards.question: How do communication satellites help you use GPS or watch satellite TV?
choices: They orbit Earth and relay signals to and from the ground
They are located on the Moon
They use magnets to send signals
cards.explanation: Satellites orbit Earth and relay radio signals across huge distances, enabling GPS, TV, and communication.
cards.realWorldExample: Your phone's map app calculates your location using signals from at least 4 GPS satellites simultaneously.
cards.funFact: There are over 8,000 active satellites currently orbiting Earth!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: The Red Planet
cards.question: Why does Mars appear reddish in the sky?
choices: It reflects red light from the Sun only
cards.explanation: Mars's surface is covered in iron oxide dust — essentially rust — giving it a reddish color.
cards.realWorldExample: NASA's Mars rovers, like Perseverance, study this rusty soil to understand the planet's history.
cards.funFact: Mars has the largest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons — nearly 3 times taller than Mount Everest!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Our Galaxy
cards.question: What is the name of the galaxy that contains our Solar System?
cards.explanation: Our Solar System is located in one of the spiral arms of the Milky Way galaxy.
cards.realWorldExample: On a clear, dark night away from city lights, you can actually see part of the Milky Way as a hazy band across the sky.
cards.funFact: The Milky Way contains an estimated 100–400 billion stars — and our Sun is just one of them!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: The Asteroid Belt
cards.question: Where is the main asteroid belt located in our solar system?
cards.explanation: The asteroid belt is a region between Mars and Jupiter containing millions of rocky leftover objects from the solar system's early formation.
cards.realWorldExample: Space missions like NASA's Dawn have visited asteroids in this belt, like Ceres and Vesta, to study the solar system's early history.
cards.funFact: Despite movies showing ships weaving through packed rocks, the asteroid belt is actually mostly empty space — the asteroids are millions of km apart!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Rovers on Mars
cards.question: Why do space agencies send robotic rovers to explore Mars instead of sending astronauts directly?
choices: Robots are cheaper and can survive Mars's harsh conditions without needing food, air, or a return trip
Mars has no interesting features to study
Rovers can fly faster than rockets
It is purely a marketing choice
cards.explanation: Robotic rovers can operate for years in Mars's extreme cold and radiation without life support, food, or a costly return journey — much safer and cheaper than sending humans today.
cards.realWorldExample: NASA's Perseverance rover has been exploring Mars, collecting rock samples and even testing how to produce oxygen there for future human missions.
cards.funFact: Signals take several minutes to travel between Mars and Earth, so rovers must be able to make some decisions on their own without instant remote control!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Life Cycle of Stars
cards.question: What eventually happens to a star much more massive than our Sun at the end of its life?
cards.explanation: Massive stars end their lives in a dramatic supernova explosion, sometimes leaving behind a neutron star or black hole.
cards.realWorldExample: Many heavy elements on Earth, like gold and iron, were originally forged inside stars and scattered by supernovas.
cards.funFact: You are literally made of "star stuff" — the calcium in your bones came from ancient exploding stars!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Black Holes
cards.question: Why can't even light escape from a black hole?
choices: Their gravity is so strong it exceeds the speed of light needed to escape
They absorb light like a sponge
cards.explanation: A black hole's gravity is so intense that the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light — nothing, not even light, can escape.
cards.realWorldExample: In 2019, scientists captured the first-ever photo of a black hole's shadow using a network of telescopes worldwide.
cards.funFact: There is a supermassive black hole at the center of our own Milky Way galaxy, called Sagittarius A*!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Exoplanets
cards.question: How do astronomers often detect planets orbiting other, distant stars?
choices: By observing tiny dips in starlight as a planet passes in front
By hearing radio signals from aliens
They cannot detect them at all
cards.explanation: The "transit method" detects a slight, regular dimming of a star's light when a planet passes in front of it.
cards.realWorldExample: NASA's Kepler and TESS space telescopes have discovered thousands of exoplanets using this exact technique.
cards.funFact: Over 5,500 exoplanets have been confirmed so far, and some are in their star's "habitable zone"!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: The Big Bang
cards.question: What evidence supports the idea that the universe is expanding?
choices: Distant galaxies show redshifted light, moving away from us
cards.explanation: Redshift (light stretching toward red wavelengths) in distant galaxies shows they are moving away — evidence for an expanding universe.
cards.realWorldExample: This redshift evidence is a cornerstone of the Big Bang theory, first observed by Edwin Hubble in 1929.
cards.funFact: The universe is estimated to be about 13.8 billion years old!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Escape Velocity
cards.question: Why must rockets reach a specific minimum speed (~11.2 km/s) to leave Earth permanently?
choices: To overcome Earth's gravitational pull entirely
cards.explanation: Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed so an object's kinetic energy overcomes Earth's gravitational pull without further propulsion.
cards.realWorldExample: Every mission sending probes beyond Earth orbit, like to Mars or the Moon, must calculate and reach this escape velocity.
cards.funFact: The Moon's escape velocity is only 2.4 km/s — over 4 times lower than Earth's — one reason lunar launches use less fuel!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: Dark Matter
cards.question: Why do scientists believe there is "dark matter" in the universe, even though it cannot be seen directly?
choices: It was invented for science fiction stories
Galaxies spin in ways that only make sense if extra unseen mass is present, pulling with gravity
It is just empty space with a strange name
Telescopes are simply too weak to see it
cards.explanation: Galaxies rotate faster than the visible matter alone can explain — extra unseen mass (dark matter) must be adding gravity to hold them together.
cards.realWorldExample: Studying dark matter's gravity even helps astronomers map where invisible mass is hiding, by observing how it bends light from objects behind it.
cards.funFact: Scientists estimate dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe — while all the stars, planets, and everything visible make up less than 5%!

cards.subject: astronomy
cards.title: The Goldilocks Zone
cards.question: What makes a distant exoplanet a promising candidate for hosting life, according to the "habitable zone" idea?
choices: It must be the largest planet around its star
It orbits at a distance where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist
It must be closest to its star
It must have rings like Saturn
cards.explanation: The habitable ("Goldilocks") zone is the orbital distance where a planet is not too hot or too cold, allowing liquid water — considered essential for life as we know it — to exist on its surface.
cards.realWorldExample: Earth sits comfortably in the Sun's habitable zone, which is a major reason it has oceans and supports life, unlike scorching Venus or frozen Mars.
cards.funFact: Scientists have found several Earth-sized exoplanets in their star's habitable zone, including some in the TRAPPIST-1 system, just 40 light-years away!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: See-Through or Not?
cards.question: Which of these lets light pass straight through it, so you can see clearly?
cards.explanation: Clear glass is transparent — light passes straight through it, letting you see what is on the other side.
cards.realWorldExample: Windows, spectacles, and water bottles are all made of transparent materials for this reason.
cards.funFact: Frosted glass in bathrooms is "translucent" — it lets light through but scrambles it so you cannot see shapes clearly!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Telling Time
cards.question: What tool do you look at to find out what time it is?
cards.explanation: A clock measures and displays time using hands or numbers that move at a steady, regular pace.
cards.realWorldExample: You check a clock to know when to leave for school or when your favourite show starts.
cards.funFact: Before clocks, people used the position of the sun in the sky to guess the time of day!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: A Full Day
cards.question: How many hours are there in one full day?
cards.explanation: A day is measured as 24 hours — split into daytime hours and nighttime hours on a clock face.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why a clock face shows 12 numbers but each number is passed twice — once for AM, once for PM.
cards.funFact: A day on Earth is exactly this long because that is how fast our planet spins once on its axis!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Where Light Comes From
cards.question: Which of these makes its OWN light, instead of just reflecting light from somewhere else?
cards.explanation: The Sun is a light source — it produces its own light. Mirrors, moons, and spoons only bounce light that already exists.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why the Moon looks bright at night — it is only reflecting sunlight, not glowing on its own.
cards.funFact: Fireflies are one of the very few living things that can make their own light too!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Days of the Week
cards.question: How many days are there in one week?
cards.explanation: A week has 7 days, and it repeats over and over to help us organise school days, weekends, and plans.
cards.realWorldExample: Your school timetable and weekend plans are both built around this 7-day repeating pattern.
cards.funFact: The 7-day week is thousands of years old — ancient Babylonians used it because they tracked 7 objects moving in the sky!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Bouncing Light
cards.question: Why can you see yourself in a mirror?
choices: The mirror creates a copy of you
Light bounces off you and reflects back off the mirror
cards.explanation: Light reflects off your face and body, hits the smooth mirror surface, and bounces back to your eyes in an orderly way.
cards.realWorldExample: Rear-view mirrors in cars and bathroom mirrors both work using this same simple reflection.
cards.funFact: A flat mirror always shows you flipped left-to-right, which is why reading text in a mirror looks backwards!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Stopwatch Precision
cards.question: Why do sports races use a stopwatch instead of a normal wall clock?
choices: A stopwatch can measure very small fractions of a second precisely
Wall clocks are too heavy to carry
cards.explanation: A stopwatch can start, stop, and measure down to hundredths of a second, which matters when races are won by a tiny margin.
cards.realWorldExample: Olympic 100m sprints are often decided by less than a tenth of a second, measured by precision timers.
cards.funFact: Some Olympic races are now timed by lasers and cameras that catch differences of one thousandth of a second!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Fast Light
cards.question: Compared to sound, how fast does light travel?
choices: About the same speed as sound
Light does not travel, it just appears
cards.explanation: Light travels about a million times faster than sound, which is why we see something happen before we hear it.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why you see lightning flash instantly but hear the thunder rumble a few seconds later.
cards.funFact: You can estimate how far away a storm is by counting seconds between the lightning flash and the thunder!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Why Things Have Colour
cards.question: A red apple looks red because the apple's skin does what to light?
choices: Absorbs all colours except red, which it reflects
Has no effect on light at all
cards.explanation: White light contains all colours. The apple's skin absorbs most colours but reflects red light back to your eyes.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why a black T-shirt feels hotter in the sun — black absorbs nearly all colours of light as heat, reflecting almost none.
cards.funFact: A banana looks yellow in white light, but under pure red light it would look almost black — no yellow light to reflect!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Time Zones
cards.question: Why is it daytime in India while it is still nighttime in New York?
choices: They use different clocks that run at different speeds
The Earth is round and spinning, so different places face the Sun at different times
New York has less sunlight overall
It is a mistake in the calendar
cards.explanation: As the round Earth spins, different regions face the Sun at different moments, so the world is split into time zones a few hours apart.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why a video call between friends in India and the USA has to be planned carefully around the time difference.
cards.funFact: There are about 24 main time zones around the globe, roughly one for every hour of Earth's rotation!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Angle of Reflection
cards.question: When light hits a flat mirror at 30° from the surface, at what angle does it bounce off?
cards.explanation: The law of reflection states the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection — light bounces off at the same angle it arrived.
cards.realWorldExample: Periscopes in submarines use precisely angled mirrors to redirect light around corners using this exact law.
cards.funFact: Skateboarders and pool players use this same "equal angle" idea to bank a ball or trick off a ramp!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Why the Sky is Blue
cards.question: Why does the daytime sky look blue instead of another colour?
choices: Air molecules scatter blue light from sunlight more than other colours
The ocean reflects its colour upward
Blue is the only colour the Sun makes
cards.explanation: Sunlight contains all colours, but tiny air molecules scatter shorter blue wavelengths much more than red or yellow, filling the sky with blue light.
cards.realWorldExample: At sunset, sunlight travels through more atmosphere, scattering away the blue and leaving the reds and oranges you see.
cards.funFact: On the Moon, which has no atmosphere to scatter light, the sky always looks black — even in daytime!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Measuring Time Without Batteries
cards.question: How does an old-fashioned hourglass measure a fixed amount of time?
choices: It counts using a hidden battery
A fixed amount of sand takes a steady, repeatable time to fall through a narrow gap
cards.explanation: Because sand flows through the narrow neck at a roughly constant rate, the same quantity of sand always takes about the same time to empty.
cards.realWorldExample: Board games like Pictionary still use sand timers today for exactly this reliable, battery-free timing.
cards.funFact: Before mechanical clocks, sailors used hourglasses at sea to time their ship's speed and navigation!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Speed of Light Number
cards.question: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
cards.explanation: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second in a vacuum — fast enough to circle the Earth over 7 times in one second.
cards.realWorldExample: GPS satellites must account for this speed extremely precisely, or your phone's map location would drift off by kilometres.
cards.funFact: Nothing with mass can travel as fast as light — it is the universe's ultimate speed limit!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Reaction Time
cards.question: Why do video game and sports athletes train their "reaction time"?
choices: To shorten the time between seeing something and reacting to it
cards.explanation: Reaction time is the tiny time gap between your senses detecting something and your muscles responding — training can shorten it slightly.
cards.realWorldExample: A goalkeeper saving a fast penalty kick, or a sprinter leaving the blocks at the starting gun, both rely on fast reaction time.
cards.funFact: The average human reaction time is about 0.25 seconds — which is why false-starting before a race gun fires gets you disqualified!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Dispersion in a Prism
cards.question: When white light passes through a glass prism and splits into colours, what causes this splitting?
choices: Different colours of light bend by different amounts inside the glass
cards.explanation: Each colour of light bends (refracts) by a slightly different amount as it enters and exits the glass, spreading white light into a spectrum.
cards.realWorldExample: This same splitting of light by water droplets is exactly why rainbows appear after rain.
cards.funFact: Isaac Newton was the first to prove that white light is actually a mixture of all the rainbow colours, using a simple prism!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Light-Speed Delay
cards.question: Why is there a noticeable delay when talking to someone via a satellite phone call, even though signals travel at light speed?
choices: Satellites are slow to process sound
The physical distance to a satellite and back is large enough for even light-speed signals to take a fraction of a second
Satellite phones use sound waves, not light
cards.explanation: Even at light speed, a signal travelling tens of thousands of kilometres up to a satellite and back takes a measurable fraction of a second.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why live TV interviews via satellite sometimes show a short awkward pause before the person answers.
cards.funFact: Signals to Mars take between 4 and 24 minutes one-way, depending on the planets' positions — real-time conversation with Mars is impossible!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Total Internal Reflection
cards.question: How does a fibre-optic cable carry light signals around bends without the light escaping?
choices: The cable is perfectly straight, never bent
Light reflects entirely off the inside walls of the cable at certain angles, trapping it inside
It uses tiny mirrors placed every centimetre
The light travels as sound instead
cards.explanation: At the right angle, light hitting the boundary between two materials reflects completely instead of escaping — called total internal reflection.
cards.realWorldExample: This exact principle carries internet and phone data as light pulses through fibre-optic cables under oceans, connecting continents.
cards.funFact: A single fibre-optic cable strand, thinner than a human hair, can carry many times more data than old copper cables!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: How Atomic Clocks Work
cards.question: What makes atomic clocks the most accurate timekeeping devices ever built?
choices: They count extremely regular vibrations of atoms instead of springs or pendulums
They are powered by nuclear reactors
cards.explanation: Atomic clocks measure the incredibly steady, predictable vibrations of atoms (like caesium) to define a second more precisely than any mechanical clock.
cards.realWorldExample: GPS satellites carry atomic clocks — without their precision, your phone's location could be off by kilometres instead of metres.
cards.funFact: An atomic clock is so precise it would not lose or gain a single second in over 100 million years!

cards.subject: lighttime
cards.title: Time Dilation
cards.question: According to Einstein's theory of relativity, what happens to time for someone travelling extremely fast compared to someone standing still?
choices: Time speeds up equally for everyone
Time passes more slowly for the fast-moving traveller
cards.explanation: Einstein showed that time is not fixed — it runs slightly slower for objects moving very fast relative to an observer, an effect called time dilation.
cards.realWorldExample: GPS satellites, moving fast and experiencing weaker gravity, actually have their onboard clocks tick at a very slightly different rate than clocks on Earth — engineers must correct for it daily.
cards.funFact: Astronauts on the International Space Station age a tiny fraction of a second less than people on Earth, due to their speed!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Electricity Like Water
cards.question: Electric current flowing through a wire is a bit like what flowing through a pipe?
cards.explanation: Just like water flows through a pipe, electric current flows through a wire — it is a useful way to picture something you cannot see.
cards.realWorldExample: Plumbers control water flow with taps, just like switches control electric current flow in a circuit.
cards.funFact: Scientists even measure electric current in "amperes", similar to how you might measure water in litres per second!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: What a Battery Gives
cards.question: What does a battery provide to push electric current around a circuit?
cards.explanation: A battery provides voltage — an electrical "push" that drives current through the circuit, similar to a pump pushing water.
cards.realWorldExample: A bigger battery (like in a car) gives a bigger push, which is why it can power much larger devices than a small toy battery.
cards.funFact: A single AA battery gives about 1.5 volts of push — a car battery gives about 12 volts, 8 times as much!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Slowing Down Current
cards.question: What word describes something that makes it harder for electric current to flow through it?
cards.explanation: Resistance is how much a material pushes back against electric current — high resistance means current flows less easily.
cards.realWorldExample: The thin wire inside a toaster has high resistance, which is exactly why it heats up and glows when current flows through it.
cards.funFact: Thick wires generally have less resistance than thin wires — that's why big electrical cables are so thick!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: More Batteries, More Push
cards.question: If you put two batteries together in a toy instead of one, what usually happens to the toy?
choices: It usually runs faster or brighter
cards.explanation: Two batteries connected the right way add up their voltage, giving a bigger push of current, which often makes toys run faster or lights shine brighter.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why some toy cars need 2 or 4 batteries instead of just 1 — more push for more power.
cards.funFact: Put batteries in backwards, though, and their pushes can cancel out instead of adding up!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Thick vs Thin Wire
cards.question: Which wire would usually let electric current flow through it more easily?
choices: They are always exactly the same
cards.explanation: A thick, short wire has lower resistance than a thin, long one, so current flows through it more easily — like a wide pipe letting more water through.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why the main cables bringing electricity into your house are much thicker than the tiny wires inside a phone charger.
cards.funFact: Overloading a thin wire with too much current can make it dangerously hot — that is exactly why fuses exist!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Measuring Current
cards.question: What unit do we use to measure how much electric current is flowing?
cards.explanation: Electric current is measured in amperes, often shortened to "amps" — named after French scientist André-Marie Ampère.
cards.realWorldExample: A hairdryer might use about 10 amps, while a small LED torch uses a tiny fraction of an amp.
cards.funFact: A household circuit breaker is often labelled "15A" or "20A" — that's the maximum current it allows before switching off!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Measuring Voltage
cards.question: What unit do we use to measure the electrical "push" (voltage) of a battery or socket?
cards.explanation: Voltage is measured in volts, named after Alessandro Volta, who invented the first battery.
cards.realWorldExample: A wall socket in India supplies about 230 volts — far more push than a small 1.5-volt battery.
cards.funFact: This much higher household voltage is exactly why you should never touch wall sockets with wet hands or metal objects!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Measuring Resistance
cards.question: What unit is used to measure electrical resistance?
cards.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms (symbol Ω), named after Georg Ohm, who studied how current, voltage, and resistance relate.
cards.realWorldExample: A resistor used in electronic circuits might be labelled "220 ohms" or "1000 ohms" depending on how much it resists current.
cards.funFact: The ohm symbol (Ω) is actually the Greek letter omega — chosen partly because it looks a little like a horseshoe magnet!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Why Wires Get Warm
cards.question: Why does an electric heater's coil glow hot when current flows through it, but a thick copper wire nearby stays cool?
choices: The coil is made of a different colour
The coil has much higher resistance, so it converts more electrical energy into heat
The copper wire is too far from the switch
cards.explanation: Materials with higher resistance convert more electrical energy into heat as current pushes through them, which is exactly how heaters are designed to work.
cards.realWorldExample: Toasters, hair straighteners, and electric kettles all use high-resistance coils on purpose, to turn electricity into heat.
cards.funFact: This heating effect is called "resistive heating" — it is also the reason overloaded plug sockets can become a fire risk!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Why Voltage Can Be Dangerous
cards.question: Why is it far more dangerous to touch a high-voltage power line than a small 9-volt battery?
choices: High voltage looks scarier but is not actually different
A much bigger push of current is driven through your body, which can seriously injure or kill
There is no real danger difference
cards.explanation: Higher voltage drives a much larger, more dangerous current through a conductive path like the human body, which is why high-voltage lines are so hazardous.
cards.realWorldExample: This is exactly why power line workers wear thick insulated gloves and suits, and why warning signs near substations say "Danger: High Voltage".
