cards.funFact: Birds can perch safely on a single high-voltage wire because current only flows when there is a path — but touching the wire and the ground (or a pole) at once completes a deadly path!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Ohm's Law in Practice
cards.question: Using Ohm's Law (V = I × R), what voltage is needed to push 2 amps of current through a 5-ohm resistor?
cards.explanation: V = I × R = 2 × 5 = 10 volts. This tells you exactly how much push is needed for a given current and resistance.
cards.realWorldExample: Engineers use this exact calculation to choose safe battery voltages for circuits with a known resistance, like an LED strip.
cards.funFact: Ohm's Law is one of the very first formulas every electronics student learns, because nearly everything else builds on it!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Electric Power Formula
cards.question: Electric power (in watts) used by a device is calculated as P = V × I. A device running on 10V and drawing 2A uses how much power?
cards.explanation: P = V × I = 10 × 2 = 20 watts. Power tells you the rate at which electrical energy is being used or converted.
cards.realWorldExample: This is exactly the formula used to calculate the wattage printed on light bulbs, chargers, and appliances.
cards.funFact: A typical smartphone charger might supply about 5V and 2A — that is 10 watts of charging power!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: How Your Electricity Bill Works
cards.question: Your electricity bill charges you based on "units" measured in kWh (kilowatt-hours). What does 1 kWh actually represent?
choices: Using 1000 watts of power for 1 hour
cards.explanation: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy — it means using 1000 watts of power continuously for one hour (or 100 watts for 10 hours, etc).
cards.realWorldExample: Running a 2000-watt heater for 1 hour uses 2 kWh — and your electricity bill charges you per kWh consumed that month.
cards.funFact: Leaving a 10-watt LED bulb on for 100 hours also uses exactly 1 kWh — the same "amount" as that heater running for half an hour!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Resistance in Series
cards.question: If you connect two 4-ohm resistors one after another (in series) in a circuit, what is their combined resistance?
cards.explanation: Resistances in series simply add up: 4 + 4 = 8 ohms — current has to push through both, one after the other.
cards.realWorldExample: Old-style string lights wired in series add up their resistance this way, which is part of why the whole string can dim if one bulb weakens.
cards.funFact: Resistors in parallel behave completely differently — their combined resistance is actually lower than either one alone!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Using a Multimeter
cards.question: An electrician uses a multimeter to check a wire. What is a multimeter designed to measure?
choices: Voltage, current, and resistance in a circuit
cards.explanation: A multimeter is a handheld tool that can measure voltage, current, and resistance, making it essential for testing and fixing circuits safely.
cards.realWorldExample: Electricians use multimeters to check if a socket is safely wired, or to find exactly where a circuit has broken.
cards.funFact: Some modern multimeters can also test batteries, diodes, and even the temperature of a component!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Resistance in Parallel
cards.question: Two identical 10-ohm resistors are connected in parallel. Is their combined resistance more or less than 10 ohms?
cards.explanation: In parallel, current has multiple paths to flow through, so the combined resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistor — here, exactly 5 ohms.
cards.realWorldExample: Household wiring is done in parallel partly because adding more devices (paths) does not multiply resistance the way series wiring would.
cards.funFact: This is also why plugging in too many parallel devices on one circuit can draw dangerously high total current, even though each device alone seems fine!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Resistance and Temperature
cards.question: For most metal conductors, what typically happens to their electrical resistance as temperature increases?
cards.explanation: As metal atoms vibrate more at higher temperatures, they get in the way of flowing electrons more often, increasing resistance.
cards.realWorldExample: This is part of why an incandescent bulb's filament briefly draws a large current the instant it is switched on cold, before heating up and its resistance rising.
cards.funFact: Superconductors are special materials whose resistance drops to exactly zero at extremely low temperatures!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law
cards.question: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law states that around any complete loop in a circuit, the total voltage supplied equals...
choices: The total voltage dropped across all components in that loop
cards.explanation: Energy is conserved around a closed loop — all the voltage supplied by sources must be exactly "used up" by the resistances in that same loop.
cards.realWorldExample: Engineers use this law to design and check circuit boards, making sure every component gets the correct voltage.
cards.funFact: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law and Current Law together let engineers analyse circuits far too complex to solve using Ohm's Law alone!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Internal Resistance
cards.question: Why does a battery's voltage often drop slightly when it powers a device that draws a lot of current?
choices: The battery itself has some internal resistance, which causes a voltage drop under load
The device steals voltage from the air
cards.explanation: Every real battery has some internal resistance, so as current increases, some voltage is "lost" inside the battery itself before reaching the circuit.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why a car's headlights can dim slightly for a moment while the starter motor draws a huge burst of current to start the engine.
cards.funFact: A battery's internal resistance also increases as it ages or gets cold, which is why old or cold batteries seem "weaker"!

cards.subject: circuits
cards.title: Why Power Lines Use High Voltage
cards.question: Why do power companies transmit electricity across long distances at very high voltages (like 400,000 volts), then reduce it before it reaches homes?
choices: For the same power, higher voltage means lower current, which loses much less energy as heat over long wires
It is a historical accident nobody has fixed
High voltage travels faster than low voltage
cards.explanation: Since power = voltage × current, transmitting at very high voltage keeps current (and resulting resistive heat loss) low, wasting far less energy over long-distance cables.
cards.realWorldExample: This is why you see large transformer stations near your neighbourhood — they safely step that high voltage back down to the ~230V used in homes.
cards.funFact: Without high-voltage transmission, a huge fraction of generated electricity would simply be wasted as heat before it ever reached your home!
